utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecution versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Representation, Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye, Ms. Soljan. Anyone else there? No. Defence teams, I already notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon. All right. I understand the Prosecution wishes to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are proposing and the Defence agrees that Mr. Parsons is here and that out of an abundance of caution we start with him just to make sure there's no risk of him going over and having to stay in for the holiday. It looks like from the estimates that we shouldn't have a problem, but as you know, sometimes we get to talking. So if we could start with Parsons and finish him, then Mr. Janc is available afterward should we have more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Janc is also available Friday, I suppose, if we need him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he is available, and that's no problem. And then I have one other preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. The other preliminary you wish to state now or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can state it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you know the Popovic team has filed a motion requesting three Bisina witnesses. We have looked at the B/C/S versions of those statements and have no objection to those statements coming in 92 bis, no cross-examination. I've discussed that briefly with Mr. Zivanovic, and so we can -- he seemed to be positive on that, though he hasn't had any time to think about it. Also with -- with Mr. Rodic, the intercept person, should we -- if we can see a brief statement or report on what he has to say, we may very well do the same thing on that issue and just let that come in through 92 bis, no cross, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Kosoric we'd like to chat with a bit. Though I would like to hear how if Mr. Kosoric is really willing to come and speak with us, because we haven't had that opportunity to speak with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. People who know me better than you do would have anticipated exactly where I was getting. All right. Thank you for that information. You will mull over it, Mr. Zivanovic, and if you are in agreement you will let us know as soon as possible. In the meantime we haven't, of course, decided on your motion, but we will be deciding soon. Thank you. Yes. Can we bring in Mr. Parsons, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Dr. Parsons, and welcome back. Could we proceed with your solemn declaration straight away, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye will put some questions to you and we'll be doing our level best to finish with your testimony today, although I don't promise. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you. Good afternoon to Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Dr. Parsons. Indeed, welcome back. As you know, you've been called back to testify for only a limited purpose on our part and of course to provide the Defence with an opportunity to cross-examine you in relation to your testimony. So I'll have not very many questions for you and then I'll turn you over to the Defence for examination. If there's anything that I say that's not clear or -- just let me know and I will rephrase it in a way that we can best understand one another and get through this in short order. You last testified over a year ago in this case. Could you just briefly tell us what your position is with the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I am the director of forensic sciences at the ICMP and oversee three main divisions or areas of speciality. One is a DNA laboratory system. Another is anthropological examinations and archaeological excavations; and the third is a central identification unit where the samples come in and identifications are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your supervisory functions, do your responsibilities include personally reviewing all of the forensic work that is carried out in ICMP labs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, they do not. The details of each and every report are not something that I normally review.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are those -- are those details reviewed -- is there an apparatus or a mechanism by which those details are reviewed in the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, particularly with regard to the DNA reports we have a very formal system of -- of review.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us just by establishment, not by name, who is responsible for reviewing the laboratory work that goes on in the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: An individual associated with the genetic analysis department, an individual associated with a statistical calculations and then the head of the DNA laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are all those aspects necessary in order to carry out adequate and appropriate testing pursuant to the certification that the ICMP has -- accreditation that the ICMP has?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, the accreditation calls for formal review processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, since you last testified are you aware of any further or updated information that the ICMP has provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in particular, can you tell us what material you are aware of that has been provided?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The primary document is an update of the DNA notification list, I believe it's as of January 2009, that lists the DNA match reports that have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you provide -- has ICMP provided any other documentation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Has ICMP provided any other documentation that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: There's a list of unmatched DNA profiles as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to look at that material or review that material recently?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And how recently have you reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's extremely voluminous, so I can't say that I've reviewed it in extreme detail, but I have familiarised myself with it recently in the last few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how was that material provided to you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: In the same form that -- that was provided to the ICTY, in Excel spreadsheets. There is an additional set of information that our -- our agency has passed to the court as well, and that is the number of case files that were requested that contain the actual DNA data, the statistical calculations and the match reports themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could have in e-court, please, 65 ter 4497. Just for the record, Your Honours, the spreadsheet of ICMP data that the witness refers to is contained in D0002768, 65 ter 4494.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, do you recognise this document that's in e-court now? And we'll go to the next page in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this a document that was provided by the ICMP to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could go, please, to the page ending 630. It should be, I guess, ten pages from here in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document, please. That would be 65 ter 4498. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this a document that was provided by the ICMP to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't put on the record the last document, the title of the document was Summary Report Cancari Road 4, BiH, ICMP site code: T-ZVO.CR04. This document reads Cancari -- Summary Report Cancari Road 06, BiH, ICMP site code: T-ZVR.CR06, and on this document if we could just go to page ending 315. It's page 10 in -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on this document, Dr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next document, which is 65 ter 4499.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record this document reads summary report, Cancari Road 08, BiH, ICMP site code: T-ZVO.CR08. And if we could just go to page ending 665, page 10 also of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature here?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to these last three documents and the spreadsheet that you referred to earlier, those were all documents that were provided by ICMP to the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the first document that you referred to, that is the document concerning the identifications -- or update of identifications that were made by the ICMP, did you have an opportunity to review all of the material in that -- in that spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say I was able to review all that material. There's over 10.000 line entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware of any particular problems or issues concerning the reliability or validity of the data that is contained in that spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Fundamentally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if I could, could I show you, please, 65 ter 4526. Are you aware of an e-mail that was provided by an employee of the ICMP on 24 April of which addressed certain -- certain issues concerning this -- this updated material?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how were you made aware of that particular -- of this e-mail?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: It was shared to me prior to its distribution and I've reviewed it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in this e-mail, as we can see under -- just near the middle --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can blow that up where it says number 1. It's right in the middle of the paragraph. Yes. Right there. I suppose everybody can read it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But could you tell us what the thrust of this e-mail is, what it concerns?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, the -- the primary list that -- that this refers to, these some 10.000 or so entries into the notification list represent DNA reports that have been made by the ICMP, and those are matches either of a victim sample to a family -- a set of families associated with a missing person, or they're related to reassociating two different parts of the same victim individual. Okay. And so it is not, strictly speaking, a list of closed cases at the ICMP, where bodies have been returned to the families. These are DNA match reports with high statistical surety ascribe an individual name to a victim sample. So it was brought to our attention as -- out of these 10.000 or so entries that are either primary matches or reassociation matches that there were a number of cases where there were apparent inconsistencies with regard to who was listed on the DNA match report, and I believe that was a list of some eight cases that required a bit of additional investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: And these -- these numbered points here reflect a number of explanations as to how something like that could occur. So a primary instance might be that we have a DNA match report, and it indicates an individual with a certain name, and then we have a set of victim remains to which this sample is thought to relate. Well, upon inspection, it turns out that it could be that the named individual is not consistent with the set of victim remains, and so I list three reasons why such an extremely rare event might -- that might cause an extremely rare event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the three reasons that you list are set out in this e-mail, is that right, under number 1, 2, and 3?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in respect of the data that you looked at, that is the most recent identification data on the spreadsheets as you've indicated, are you aware that any one of these particular circumstances has in fact occurred, or are these an explanation of potential or possible explanations for the discrepancies that were pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: In the cases in question, in fact we remain to identify the root cause of which -- which of these three or -- or possibly another explanation might be. In fact, in one case I made reference to another explanation, and in one case we did determine that that was the case, and that was that we have two identical twins whose DNA was exactly the same between them, and therefore they were -- they were matched to the -- to the same name, and as we later found out, they were the twins and we were able to sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you aware of any defects in the testing procedures that were -- that are employed by the ICMP or were employed by the ICMP that would call into question the reliability of the results that are -- that are shown in the spreadsheet of identifications as you referred to previously? That is, are you aware of any defects in the testing procedures themselves?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: With regard to the actual DNA typing and methodology, I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And would the explanations that you've given here for these rare instances, as you've referred to them, would these kinds of individualised errors impact on the overall reliability and accuracy of the results that have been obtained by ICMP in respect of identifications?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: In -- in some ways, yes, and in some ways, no, and that's obviously something I would have to clarify. The -- the DNA match reports that are contained in that list and -- indicate the DNA that was obtained from a victim sample, and I would say in -- in every case, regardless of these -- these very small number of cases we're discussing here, even including those, the sample that was tested for DNA in fact matches that family and that named individual as it is stated on the match report. The problem comes in with correlating that sample to where it was originally thought to have been taken from. So we have a small number of cases where there was potentially, for example, a labelling error when the sample was taken usually by an outside agency, not the ICMP. If the proper code was not written on that to allow it to refer back to the body, then there would be a discrepancy when the DNA report was compared to the remains that it was written down it came from. Certainly the DNA profile and the DNA match we got from the sample itself is correct. It's simply due to, if you will, a clerical error at some point in the process is no longer ascribed to the set of remains that -- that we hoped to return to the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are there any systemic or systematic problems in -- in the handling or administratively or even in the laboratory context of data or samples within the ICMP that, in your view, might imperil the validity or reliability of the ICMP results?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: In terms of systematic problems, no. In fact, the system is very carefully designed to control -- to avoid these problems, and -- and as a result, in any given case the chance of a problem such as this is extremely minuscule.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple of questions. As you mentioned concerning some case files, could you tell us a little bit about that? You mentioned that the ICMP had provided some case files.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe you're referring to -- to it a number of cases that were requested by the Office of the Prosecutor to provide the underlying DNA data and associated documents for -- for review.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you oversee the compilation of this material?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That would not be a role that I would play directly, no. That would be -- that requires a great deal of -- of collation of material and -- and background research by the staff that actually conduct the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware of -- are you aware of the circumstances under which this material was gathered, that is, what is it -- what it relates to, when it was put together, what it comprises?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell us a little bit about that, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, having -- having had these particular cases brought to our attention, we then had to access the records we have on the matching processes, access the raw data on computer files in the laboratory, check to see that -- that everything is included and assemble them all together. An additional very time-consuming element of this process was to obtain victim consent waivers. In other words, consent from the family members involved in these DNA match reports to have their DNA profiles and their personal information released to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain these consent forms or consents of the victims, I should say, or relatives in all instances?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. I believe there were a number of cases where that simply was not possible. That is to say that the families refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And approximately, if you know, how many case files did the ICMP compile?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: You know, I apologise, but I don't happen to know that number right off the top of my head. It's around 25 or something if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware if there were any difficulties in compiling these -- this information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Not fundamentally, no. We were able to provide the DNA information for -- for all the cases and the matches that they were -- they were -- they were based on. In some instances, to ensure that we were providing the proper information, we did -- we did actually quickly retype a couple of the blood samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. When you say retype, you're speaking in a scientific sense and not in a colloquial literal sense of actually typing as in a typewriter; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm referring to is that -- that the genetic profiles from the reference blood samples were in some cases obtained many, many years ago prior to 2003 or in that era, and some of the criteria were slightly different for -- for how we go about designating these profiles. So to be safe and conservative, we retyped them again according to current-day standards and I'm pleased to report that there weren't differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of evaluating the reliability of the DNA analysis procedures that you follow, is it possible in the absence of examining electropherograms, is it possible to determine whether or not a DNA analysis or procedure is a valid and reliable one?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, if you have access to the raw data such as we provided here, someone should be able to look at those and say they've been drawn on solid conclusions. I would like to qualify that, though, by saying that nothing exists in a vacuum, so it -- it would also be with -- the expert reviewing this material, it would also be within his knowledge that this is in fact an extremely well-established, fundamental means for DNA typing that has emerged as a gold standard in forensic analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are there other factors that might reasonably be considered in order to evaluate the reliability of a lab practice and the results that are obtained by a particular or a given lab?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. It relates to many things. One would be the -- the level of experience and training within the laboratory, and in that regard, ours is one -- one of the world's most highly experienced laboratory. It would go to quality control procedures that have been well-devised and implemented and documented, as is currently the case in our laboratory. And it would be -- it would go to accreditation standards. Our laboratory is inspected very formally by outside, neutral investigators to determine that our processes map onto our protocols and vice versa. And then lastly, the extent to which that laboratory works in concert with the -- with other workers in the field, other experts in the field, in other words, the extent to which we maintain state-of-the-art capabilities that are up-to-date. And we have in that regard a scientific advisory board of many of the more prominent scientists in the world that on a yearly basis come in and review our processes and help us discuss where we are and how -- how the processes fit in with the state of the art worldwide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And lastly, in your view, do you have any concerns regarding the reliability or validity of the data that's been provided by the ICMP to the Office of the Prosecutor as concerns the DNA analysis procedures and the results that they show?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't. I think they're rock solid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Dr. Parsons. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic will lead this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I apologise. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Parsons. I hope you remember that in February last year we had an opportunity to conduct a conversation, so we're going to continue that here today, but we're going to talk today in line of the Trial Chamber's decision and ruling, which is that your testimony will be to authenticate some new facts about DNA identification to which investigator Janc, who attached his resume here, to which he -- on which he relies. Now, you mentioned just now, you said there were some new documents with respect to the time when you testified last year or, rather, that the only new document was an updated list of missing persons which was compiled, as you said, I think, in January of this year and afterwards sent to the Prosecutor, to the OTP. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, as I -- as I just mentioned, also we provided some case files, but that is -- the list you just referred to is the primary thing, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in the meantime, during the space of that year, you have changed any SOP or standard operative procedure which you applied in the process of establishing the identity of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The answer would be yes. We very often will modify our SOPs. In this case, in quite minor ways, but it would be the case that one would expect some of those to have been updated in terms of very narrow procedural manipulations, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And these new operative procedures, did you send them to the Prosecutor? Have you provided them? Or can I put this question a different way: Have you informed the OTP that you've changed any of the standard operative procedures?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, we certainly don't inform the OTP every time we change a procedure in the laboratory, and I think that the OTP is aware that many of our procedures will be updated regularly as is the case in all laboratories. I think it's rather important in this context to note that fundamentally the type and quality of testing that we do in the laboratory hasn't changed at all. So it's not as if we've employed new techniques. It's a simple change in -- in some operating procedures at a very detailed level.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, these new operative procedures just promote the way in which you work without influencing the quality of your work. Would that being correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think that's a reasonable statement, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since the time you testified last year, the Prosecutor on several occasions disclosed to us raw material, if I can use the term, or the match reports support documentation files. Now, you know that the Defence of -- that the Popovic Defence, and I'm a member of that Defence team, asked the ICP to provide them with all the basic raw material. Asked the ICMP, actually.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the Prosecutor disclosed this raw material to us relating to 30 cases and that all the cases relate to a locality called Bisina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm sure you're also aware that in that locality a total of 39 bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I would not know that off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know that the Prosecution disclosed to us 30, if I can call them sets or groups of raw material for 30 out of the total of 39 victims that were exhumed at the Bisina locality?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I accept that prompt to my recollection, yes. That seems correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does your answer mean, sir, that you personally did not conduct a selection, did not make a selection of which raw material of those 39 exhumed persons from Bisina locality be sent to the Prosecution and, in turn, disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us within the frameworks of the ICMP who was in charge and responsible for making the selection of these 30 out of the total of 39 Bisina cases?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, my previous answer reflects mostly the fact that no one at the ICMP selected which ones to provide and which ones not. If I may clarify. It was in regard to which ones that within the ICMP policies we were able to provide by virtue of having appropriate waivers from the family members involved in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in all the 39 cases for Bisina agreement was asked from the family for disclosing information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe so, ma'am, but I will say that an effort was made to ask all the families. I can't -- I can't, as I sit here, assure you that, for example, we had appropriate contact information for each and every one, but I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Now, can you tell us whether these 30 samples out of a total of 39 for Bisina is a sufficiently representative sample to be able to -- for people to be able to make a conclusion as to the correctness of the work of the ICMP with respect to identification? Is that a sufficiently large sample?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The issue of -- you're asking fundamentally a statistical question, I believe, and the answer to any sample-size question or issue, is to what degree of certainty and what level of precision are you trying to talk about. If you're asking do these 30 cases prove clearly that ICMP has never made a mistake, obviously that is -- that's not sufficient to be supported. If -- if the review of 30 cases is conducted, one could certainly conclude that on the basis of that information that the general standard of testing in the laboratory is of a very high level and there is no indication within that sample for doubt as to an identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor provided us with the complete documentation relating to the exhumations at Bisina and the ruling from the Cantonal Court Bisina for the exhumation in Bisina, and all the other relevant material relating to the autopsy of those bodies. But tell me now, please, do you know that the identification process was conducted mostly in 2007 for Bisina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have to say in fact that I don't know when the identifications were concluded. My understanding is that the DNA match reports -- the finalisation of the DNA match reports was relatively recent in these cases. I would have to refer to the dates on the files, ma'am. 2007 seems reasonable to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that the Prosecution provided us with that data, I meant that it was all part of the exhibits with the numbers 4510 to 4521. That's information for the benefit of the rest of the people in the court here. But can you tell me, please, Mr. Parsons, whether you know the exact number of persons identified during 2007 and during 2008 as well?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the number can be established, can it not, through the tables and the tracking charts that -- issued by the ICMP; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the proceedings so far, on two occasions we introduced these tracking charts.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for my colleagues they are Exhibits P3488 and 3D461. The first tracking chart which I mentioned is dated March, and the second dates to August 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, Mr. Parsons, in these tracking charts, among other things, you show the number of samples, blood samples, taken up until the date when the tracking chart was issued; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Is it possible to review these documents, refer to them as I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. By all means, Mr. Parsons -- Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance. It was indeed my intention to pull them up on e-court. So may we have document number 1D1376 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, in this document, which is on our screens, we have collected several tracking charts which you sent to the Prosecution and the Prosecution disclosed to the Defence, and I'd like to ask us to zoom down to the bottom of the document now, please, to see what it says there. Now, Mr. Parsons, can you see that here on the document it says that it was issued -- or, rather, that the information was updated on the 20th of February, 2009?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the top of the document now, please, the beginning of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you answer my question now, please, Mr. Parsons, and it was whether in these tracking charts we see the total number of blood samples collected and the total number of bone samples collected.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct. The second block of -- of rows don't specifically state bone in a number of the instances, but that is -- my understanding is that is what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer. Now let's go to the last page of this document, please, if we may. We have here six tracking charts, and we put them in chronological order. I'd like to ask you now --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, may we zoom down the document and see the date at the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, can you see there that it says that this document was issued on the 27th of March, 2009?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, not to go back to the first page again, the first column -- or one of the columns tells us how many DNA reports were issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can keep the document there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we go underneath the third thick black line, you'll see a column which says "Total number of reports." Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I hope you'll take me at my word and believe me if I say that we've done a mathematical report for the total number of reports between the first and last tracking chart that I've shown you. We arrive at a figure of 2.144 DNA reports. Now, do you know that on an annual level that would be a reasonable figure or is that not relevant as far as your work is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Remind me of the time period we're talking about here? I know I just looked at those dates, but I appreciate if you could refresh me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Parsons. The two tracking charts that I've just shown you incorporate the period of one year, one year exactly, perhaps with a day or two give or take, but as far as I can see from the documents, the tracking charts are issued on a weekly basis. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Parsons, we're dealing with the period of a year plus or minus two or three days, and I don't think that's important here. Now, to go back to my question. Do you know that the number of issued DNA reports for this one-year period was 2.144 based on the tracking charts that I've shown you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Parsons, these figures indicate the total number of DNA reports issued. From that can you tell us - so the number is roughly 2.000 DNA reports - of that number how many were positive DNA identifications, because a figure of 2.000 DNA reports does not mean that 2.000 persons were positively identified.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The exact answer to the question is no, I can't tell you that, but I'm willing to put forward that a vast majority of them would have been. The only time we issue non-positive DNA reports is in response to presumptive identifications and we've had a few of those, a few requests for those. It's listed here actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Thank you, but you haven't told me whether the number of reports reflects the number of positive identifications at all, and would that be 2.000?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: So I would like to ask you, please, to clarify what you mean by an identification. I think I see the nature of your question, but you're distinguishing a DNA match report from an identification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't use the terminology that you use, that's quite certain, but I'll try and simplify what I actually want to ask you to see if you understand what I'm getting at. If we have 2.144 DNA reports, the reports on identification, are they also of that number or a lesser number? Did you have as many or less?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Let me -- let me address a number of issues that I think get to what -- what you're -- what information you're interested in receiving. A DNA match report is simply the result of a DNA test. What one often considers in practice to be an identification would be the closure of a case by identification authorities of which ICMP is not one, and -- and the repatriation of that victim to the family. In -- a reason why the number of identifications as defined the way I just said, remember I said closure of a case, in other words, the entire case has been solved and considered to be resolved and then handed over to the families, the reason why that number can be smaller, and in many instances in Srebrenica is smaller than the number of DNA match reports, is that it relates to the issue of the secondary graves and the extreme fragmentation of the victims. As you're aware, there were -- primary mass graves were exhumed and buried into a series of secondary mass graves where the victims become fragmented and commingled, and therefore, entire bodies are not recovered at once from these graves. So we may get a DNA match report only on a small portion of an individual but the pathologist in question, who isn't in that role part of the ICMP, would not want to close that case, would not want to go to the family until additional portions of that individual had been identified, and that's one of the biggest challenges with the Srebrenica case, and that's why there would be a difference in those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that over that period of time you have about 2.000 DNA reports but much fewer cases.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now dwell for a while on the tracking charts. What you see now on your screen is third column from the bottom entitled "Cases Closed." Can you see this -- this column, Mr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: If we could please scroll -- go down a little bit in the document so I can see the bottom. You said the third row, I think you mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, this is now the third column from the top. It says "Cases Closed," 2.790 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, now we have to go back to the top of the document. I -- you said third from the top. No. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was on your screen at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll it a bit more and let's leave it exactly at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague, it's just that the transcript reflects the number of 2.790. If it's corrected to 3.790 it would be easier for Dr. Parsons to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye, for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do see the entry you're referring to. I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Parsons. Can you tell me what is the significance of this term "Cases Closed"? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is when the pathologist in charge of the case, that would be a court-appointed pathologist by the BiH national authorities, issues a death certificate and returns the -- the remains to the family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in your updated list of identifications marked P4494, did you in any way represent in any of the columns which particular case has been afforded the status of a case closed, that is to say, that the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina have handed over the remains of the deceased to the family, or in other words, that the death certificate was handed over to the family.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That information you just referred to is not listed in that -- in the notification list of DNA match reports, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back now again to the Bisina cases, because that's the only site for which we have full information provided in this raw material. Therefore, we are going to focus on Bisina a little more. You told us that only for Bisina, as far as I understood, sought additional consent from the families, and that you attached them, and we received them along with the material; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps seek the consent for some other sites, not only for Bisina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Not specifically retroactively with regard to provision to the court. However, our current consent forms, since well over a year now - I apologise, I don't remember the date - now have provision for the families when they provide a blood sample to give consent in the beginning for provision to the court. So we do in fact have quite a number of people -- well, it's not a huge number, but multiple family members have already given consent to have their data released to the court. But for the majority of the time that the ICMP has been in operation, when we collected the blood samples we did not have provision at that time for them to provide consent, and therefore we had to go back retroactively in these cases and specifically request it, and it's a very delicate undertaking in terms of contacting the families.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but after reviewing the documents relating to the Bisina, that is to say, the raw material provided to us by the OTP, we saw that in 30 cases -- or out of the 30 cases, consent of families members was provided in 11 cases, that is to say, from the families living abroad. For example, in the case of Sekovic 04, from Holland, from the USA, from Germany; Sekovic 029, the USA again; Sekovic 07, France, et cetera. This tells me, Mr. Parsons, that this wasn't so problematic at all, particular in view that all these consents were obtained in January and March 2009.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The fact that we have gone to the effort to find the location of, reach out to and contact people and obtain consent from people living throughout a wide number of nations, in fact attests to what great effort it did require and the amount of work that we had to go to in order to, at this late time, provide information that has been requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I presume that you have been informed that Mr. Popovic's Defence team applied directly to the ICMP last year with a request for the entire raw material relating to Srebrenica to be disclosed. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to call up this document in e-court for the sake of time saving, do you remember that in your response, although your response was signed by someone else, not yourself, I think that was Mr. Andreas Kleiser, if I pronounce his name correctly, it was said that the obtainment of consent from family members had begun in 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That was when our forms were modified so that people that we initiated contact with at that time or later would automatically be asked if they wanted to provide waivers. We did not attempt to -- any retroactive means to contact any of the other family reference samples, the many, many thousands of family reference samples, to go back to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we now see in e-court document 1D1371, but can we please not broadcast this document because it contains the name of a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. That's exactly what we will do. No broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from Exhibit 4494. It is made up of four documents that relate to the hospital in Srebrenica, but for the purpose of our discussion, I only need page 4 of the document. So can we please now move to page 4. Mr. Parsons, do you recognise the DNA report issued by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I recognise that as an ICMP DNA report. I certainly wouldn't know that one by -- by specificity.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, during our conversation today, for the sake of the protection of the integrity of the victims we are going to refrain from using any names. We shall, rather, use only numbers. However, if there are any names shown in the documents, we shall try not to broadcast them for the same reasons that I just explained to you. Let us now just move to the bottom of the document -- or, rather, the last paragraph there. Since this is very small print, I'm going to read it out to you, Mr. Parsons. "[In English] This record is privileged and confidential and shall be used in legal proceedings only for the purposes of identification unless otherwise authorised with the written consent of living person to which the record refers." [Interpretation] While we still have this document on the screen Mr. Parsons, you will see that this particular DNA report was issued in 2005.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleagues have drawn attention to me that I omitted the first sentence, and it's very short. I'm going to read it out. "[In English] This record is established by the ICMP for the sole purpose of identifying the mortal remains of missing persons." [Interpretation] What follows in this paragraph that I read out, which is apparently in the form issued by the ICMP, it says that this document can be used in legal proceedings for the purpose of identification. In these proceedings, we are conducting the procedure of identifying the victims relating to Srebrenica. Tell me now, then, why is it necessary to obtain a separate consent of the family when this document clearly shows in 2005 that this document can be used in legal proceedings for the purpose of establishing identities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I would like to preamble my answer to that by reading the final sentence in that paragraph that we've -- we've read the other parts of so far. That would be: "Other restrictions may apply. If in doubt, contact ICMP for further information." With that as a preamble, I would like to go back to -- more specifically to your question with regard to legal proceedings only for the purpose of identification. Well, it turns out that the -- the identifications that the ICMP strives to make are -- or strives to assist in making are legal identifications as determined by the death certificate. So our aim here is to provide assistance so that the families can have legal closure with relation to the identification of their loved ones. Within the ICMP's understanding and within -- within the sense of the ICMP's policies and the way -- and policies that are absolutely necessary to conducting our work, we would view the -- the legal proceedings of this court to be related to criminal prosecution, not to identification. At any rate, that is the distinction with which -- which we clearly make. That sentence, when it was written, was -- was directed toward legal processes solely associated with identification and not with criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we now see in e-court Exhibit 1D1394. And I also would kindly ask this document not to be broadcast either.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, the ICMP has had a number of different form formats in time, and I note that this is in the local language of the former Yugoslavia. If you could -- it's a consent form; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I agree with you. That is why I asked you, Mr. Parsons, if you recognised the document, because there's no translation of this document. This is a consent of family members of the donor from the Haradinaj case in which the ICMP -- or, rather, the OTP provided a full set of raw data at the request of the Defence. I'm going to read out to you, and I hope the OTP will not object to this, so that you understand what is written in this document. "International Commission for Missing Persons, ICMP, is working on the collection of blood samples from family members from the persons missing in the recent conflict in the former Yugoslavia. From these samples the ICMP will extract and process DNA data and register them on the database only for the purpose of assisting the process of identification. We are going to abide by strict rules of preservation or safeguarding of data or -- and any use of these samples for other purposes will not be allowed. The DNA donors will -- the identity of the DNA donors will remain confidential." If in the Haradinaj case the genetical material, confidential material was disclosed, which is part of the so-called genetic privacy, at the request of the Defence, this kind of consent of the donor's family member is actually disclosed, tell me, then, why is it a problem to disclose the same documents relating to Srebrenica that contain this kind of raw data without going into this complex procedure that you explained to us and that was subsequently implemented on the 30 Bisina cases?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: In the cases provided for the Haradinaj prosecution that you refer to, we went to exactly the same extensive efforts to retroactively obtain consent from the family members for exactly the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Parsons, if we review the issue of privacy and why these data are not divulged, can you tell me precisely what is the reason for this data not to be disclosed -- or, rather, why are you refusing to disclose them without additional consent? What particular reason of privacy warrants this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, there are two reasons at different levels. The first level seems quite clear. It's because, as we've just read in this document you've shown, we've already assured the donors that it would be used for no purpose. We've specifically assured individuals that it would not be used for that purpose. We are then obligated to stand by our previous statements. The reason we established the policy for that is that the ICMP needs to have the trust of the families. What we want to do is to have as many families as possible have recourse to the human rights element of being able to receive their loved ones back and know their fate, and therefore we want them to be able to participate in the process without being afraid that they might be involved in some sort of a criminal prosecution that they might otherwise not want to have anything to do with. They may not have interest in, they may be frightened of the types of things going on here, but they still want their loved ones back, and so the ICMP wanted to establish policies to permit us to do our work for the purpose of returning their family member to them without them being concerned that it would draw them in potentially without their explicit consent into proceedings related to -- such as those in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, your job stems from a war that engulfed this region, and crimes were committed on both sides. Can we then conclude that one of the reasons for the protection of privacy is that perhaps the possibility has been ruled out that some of the individuals whose identity is being established have perhaps been declared war criminals by the other warring party?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think it's conceivable that one might argue that that would be a component of some justification. I don't recall it having been a factor in our own considerations. So the answer that I gave you previously, I think, is both -- is the sufficient basis and the primary basis with which we made that policy.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that these genetical information is kept confidential because they open up possibilities for determining that some blood relations actually are nonexistent?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm fairly confident that the answer to that question is yes, but I think we need to -- to clarify what you meant by the question. Maybe if you could take another -- another try at it, or phrased slightly differently, or expand on it more clearly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In administrative and legal terms, certain persons are considered blood relatives, but once it reaches the stage of DNA matching, it turns out that they are not actually related to each other.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think -- I think I do know the sense of your question. Let me just -- just give a clarification that I'm comfortable with and then you can -- you can let me know if I'm addressing the correct issue. When one obtains genetic samples from family members, in this case as reference samples to assist with the identification of their loved ones, one obtains information about what the real genetic relationships are amongst those family members, and sometimes the actual genetic relationships are not those that are either reported to us or believed by the families, and a common -- to give an example that will clarify what I'm talking about is sometimes, as we all know, there are issues of nonpaternity, for example, and those can become apparent in the course of our work, and that in fact is an extremely good reason why we maintain absolute control over the privacy of the genetic information.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Mr. Parsons, let us now go back to the Bisina cases and the raw material supplied to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, I would kindly ask document 1D1334 to be shown in e-court and not to be broadcasts. This is a large document, some 80 pages, and it's a complete set of raw material pertaining to SEK 040 case. If we can zoom in on the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the line which says "Case number"? There is a marking, VIS 01, which is the marking for the site or the grave, SEK 40 B (Zmax). This B, I suppose, means -- stands for body?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's the -- the case number is simply a site code that is assigned outside of the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But since this is something that appears on a regular basis on all ICMP's identification lists, I'm interested in this letter B after the figure 4. I'm not asking you about the site code. I understand that this is absolutely none of our business.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I apologise. I may have misspoken. I meant the case number is assigned outside of the ICMP system. I have no information of certainty to provide you with regard to that B or any other information in the case number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's my fault, Mr. Parsons, and I wasn't precise in my question. This B after the 040, does that -- is that B for body? Does that mean that it's a body?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to page 2, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the lower left-hand corner, in the black rectangle, black box, there you'll see the sample that was taken from the body of a person who has the markings 040 B, and according to all our information, this is a tooth taken for DNA analysis, and we can see that from the report on the exhumation, and we'll look at that in just a moment? Now, when DNA analyses are conducted, Mr. Parsons, tell us, please, whether I -- or tell me whether I understand the process. There's an initial examination. Then you conduct a statistical information and then a final examination; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, those terms are not specific enough for me to quite understand what you're -- I'm not able to say yes or no to that question as stated. Are you speaking about levels of review of the -- of the findings?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly those are levels of review of findings. I'm looking at the documents that I have in front of me, but let's move on to the next page of this document. The next thing we have is the decoded DNA report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we scroll down so we can see the bottom of the document better.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, here, Mr. Parsons, where the signatures are, we have "Statistical calculation," "Initial review ," "Statistical review," and "Final review."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to, those stages. Tell me now, please, Mr. Parsons, are these reviews conducted by the same people or different people?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: In general, different people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't stop you before precisely to let you finish the chain of questions. We can have a break of 25 minutes now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic. Are we nearing the end?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I think I'll need the whole of the next session to complete my examination of Professor Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anybody else cross-examining this witness? Okay. Go ahead, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, can we continue where we left off? I was asking you about the difference between the initial review, statistical review, and final review, and I asked you whether these reviews are conducted by the same person.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Different persons, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are these reviews conducted simultaneously or at different periods?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Sequentially, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about the B and the number 040, and you said you didn't know what that stood for. Do you know what the marking BP stands for that is placed along with the numbers linked to certain victims?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I know what it means when the ICMP uses them in some cases. I don't know what it means unless I know that the ICMP has sampled the remains according to a recent SOP. I don't believe it's the case that the ICMP did any sampling here, so I will say -- I will not provide any opinion as to what B or BP means in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and we'll have to move the document to the left slightly for the next question, can you tell us, Mr. Parsons, in that black box, the first line says BIS 01 SEK 040 B and then we have Zmax 1. Do you know what this Zmax 1 stands for, means?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The same answer applies.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Now, you said that you provided the ICMP latest list of identified persons in February this year to the Prosecution, and if we look at that list, which has about 10.600 entries, you will see that almost every second or third entry has some markings in the case ID. The B, it has the B or a BP or F or Z -- rather, Z. So how is it possible if you supply this list and if you deal with identifications, you don't know what these letters stand for and they're to be found on most of the entries in the list?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Very simple answer. Those are simply the names of the samples that come to us. The ICMP didn't give those names. They could be any number of things. In fact, in the experience of the ICMP, you can imagine virtually any type of sample code. We simply do not dictate or take responsibility for what the samples are named when they come to us. They could have been named Bob and Bob would be written on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, I remember when you were testifying last year that we dealt with methodology and the work of the ICMP and the application of the standard operative procedures, SOPs, and as far as I remember, there was a standard operative procedure which related to the cleaning of teeth and bones; is that right? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to accept your answer when you say that you don't know how your institution marks a sample, which, for example, can mean a tooth sample.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Ma'am, our institution does not mark those. They come to us from outside agencies. We handled the plane crash in Cameroon. They had their own code system. We simply call it what it was called when it was given to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who then does the case ID, assigns the case ID?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Typically and probably in this case I would imagine it's the pathologist who perform the sampling.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who assigns the protocol ID?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is definitely an ICMP number. We assign that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So then I conclude that it is the -- that the ICMP is also assigned by the international commission.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have three types of annotations in each of the list of identified persons, the case ID, and you told us about that. You said you can't define who assigns this. Then you said for the protocol ID, which determines -- which is determined by your international commission, and then there is the ICMP ID. So is it the international commission which assigns an ICMP ID as well?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The ID number and the protocol number are both internally generated tracking numbers for our own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know what the case ID is composed of, how do you know what type of identification it is in each specific case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "what type of identification."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know from the documents you have and the documents I showed you whether it is a procedure of identification for main case or reassociation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: That has to do with how the DNA matches were made. So if we -- if we obtain a sample and we photo document what it is, in this case it is quite obviously a tooth, and we have a unique identifier for that. That's the case number. We don't care what it is. There is no restrictions on what that is. We obtain a DNA profile for that and then we compare it to the family references. If we get a match and a -- a determination that that sample relates to the family, then we call that the main case, because we have now put a name on a DNA -- on a sample that's been given to us. If we subsequently find another part of the same individual, we call that a reassociation, because that reassociates to a case that has previously been identified as well. So the first time we identify it it's the main case, and any additional parts of the same individual that are discovered, that are identified by DNA, become reassociation cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you told me a moment ago that from this document, the one I showed you, that you cannot establish whether it's a tooth or some other bodily part. Now you say it's a tooth. So how come you concluded that this is a tooth? On the basis of what I told you; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. There's a picture of a tooth there in the photo documentation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell us, Mr. Parsons, the document that you have before you, what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we zoom out so we could see the whole document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would like me just to describe in general what this is and its purpose, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what type of document this is. Yes, precisely as you put it.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: This is an internal ICMP DNA match report. So this is -- this is sort of the summary of the findings with regard to this case, and so what we have at the very top is the sample number as it was supplied to us. Again, nothing to do with our choosing or any requirements as to its content. The BIS 01 SEK, et cetera, that's the sample number. Beneath it is a code that we have associated with that sample for our own tracking purposes, so that's just what it gets called as it goes through the laboratory system in the computers. And then to the right of that is the DNA profile that we've obtained for the sample and that is depicted by a series of numbers that relate to things called alleles, and at any rate, we type these two alleles for each of 16 different locations in the DNA of an individual and so that's listed there. And those would reflect the findings of the electropherograms that are in the -- in the full data reports that you've received. Beneath that in the next block are additional individuals -- relate to additional individuals who are the reference families in this -- reference family members in this case. So we have a match for this sample on a particular named individual, and then that person's wife and three sons that were provided as references for that missing individual. Their genetic profiles are also listed there. And then -- so that's kind of the primary set of information by which the DNA calculations are made, and then as you noted, there's a photograph in the lower left. That represents one of the photo documentation pieces. It's just a way to indicate that we track carefully what we get in and what it relates to. And then a conclusion statement to the right that describes the results of the DNA statistical analysis that tells us the statistical surety with which the named individual can be associated with those family reference samples in the manner indicated on this report. Now, I mentioned at the outset of all of that this is an internal -- ICMP internal DNA match report and what that means is it's the one that is used for -- to complete a review process. So there are a number of levels of review. First is the signature by the individual who found this match by performing the DNA database comparisons and -- and entered it into the system. The next is the person who then took the information as represented on here and perform the statistical calculation. The third individual signed there, it says initial review, is the person -- so -- at the end of those two analyses really all the work has been done. So there is no more information to be generated in the case, but we have two additional levels of checking to review. So then we would have an initial review where someone looks over everything to say, yes, it's -- it's in order. I've -- I've checked it. It's right. We have statistical review which is a second person independently pulls the data in and regenerates the statistical calculation. This is -- this is the numerical part of it and compares it to the previous result. When that level of review is completed then it goes to one of the senior members of the laboratory, and that person reviews all the information and then -- and then signs that it appears to be correct. And so after this is done, then -- then this internal report goes back to the identification coordination division, which then generates a -- a DNA match report very similar to this one for external distribution, and the primary difference between the internal one and the externally distributed one is that in the external copy the DNA information is scrambled in a way to protect genetic privacy. I apologise if that was a lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You gave -- provided us with a detailed explanation. Tell me now, this DNA report that you have before you on the screen, is it coded or not coded?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: The one on the screen is not coded. That would be the internal one that we look at for -- so that we can check everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if on this uncoded internal report -- well, if we look at it, you mentioned the allele, and if relook at the seventh and eighth box, we have a D18 gene, S51. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can zoom into the upper left-hand corner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that Mr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the electropherogram two pages on in this same document. If we look at the fourth group of these peaks here, we'll see that it says 15, 18, and 20. That's the group, 15, 18, 20; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me -- well, on the previous page in the report, the uncoded report, you saw that in the fourth locus, in the allele, we have numbers 00.00. So may we just go back two pages to the document we were looking at earlier on. And can you tell me, please, why the values of this gene 8 -- let me read the exact number, D18S51, which in the electropherogram are marked by 15, 18, and 20, have not been included in this report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Recalled]
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, I think I have to answer no, that I could not tell you that, but what I can do is tell you what -- some general reasons why those alleles would -- why alleles are sometimes marked 00. And the reason I just don't feel like it's proper for me to be more specific is that I would have to look at more of the genetic information in this case, but -- but let me take -- take an attempt to -- to describe the -- the type of considerations that going on here and the types of things we might see. What the 00 means is that the genetic information at that locus, this D1 8, et cetera, was not deemed by the ICMP to have been accurately recovered to the level of scientific surety that we are comfortable with. So when you deal with these degraded skeletal remains that have been in harsh environments for long periods of time, it becomes a very specialised type of DNA testing, and it happens that the DNA becomes degraded over time. So the DNA becomes damaged and fragmented and attacked by microorganisms, et cetera. So because the DNA has been fragmented, sometimes it's difficult to recover the information to make these allele calls.
